newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala to privatize phone industry by next year.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala to privatize phone industry by next year.

text.p: Guatemala will privatize the state-owned telephone company Guatel and open the telecommunications market to international competitors by next year, a congressional official said Friday.
"Between December and March we could be accepting bids," said Mario Roberto Paz, chairman of the Congressional Communications Commission.
Simultaneous privatization and opening up of a telecommunications industry is unusual, but Paz said it made sense.
"The great infrastructure that (the phone company) already has set up would mean that its value would not diminish," said Paz.
The Guatemalan Telecommunications Company (Guatel in Spanish), grossed $3.8 million in international calls in the first half of 1995 and is one of the government's largest sources of income.

But Guatel's one million lines serve more than 10 million citizens, lines frequently go dead for hours or days for no apparent reason and the company doesn't have the estimated $1.1 million needed to meet the current demand for new lines.

Paz said a General Telecommunications bill, which will be presented to Congress next week, proposes an autonomous Superintendency of Telecommunications which will oversee bidding processes, regulate the industry and prices, and oversee interconnected telephone networks.
Under the new law, companies will be able to buy the rights to install new lines, to rent out lines or to provide their own telephone service. Guatel will also rent lines to service providers.
The Superintendency will make money selling rights to frequencies and to service areas. Some of that income will go to a fund to subsidize phone lines to remote areas.

The proposed law doesn't set a maximum foreign ownership of the telecommunications industry in Guatemala. Minimum investment amounts will be set for each individual frequency or area opened up for bidding, said the congressman.

Paz said he's confident the government will round up the two-thirds vote the bill needs to become law, despite party bickering currently holding up a similar law to privatize state-owned electric companies.

Currently Guatel is the country's only long-distance provider, but under the new system customers will choose local and long-distance providers. Guatel will raise its cheap local rates and lower international rates to bring them into range with future competition.
Paz said another law is being prepared to privatize Guatel and sell stock in the company. The government would remain a majority stock holder, and workers would retain five or more percent ownership.
The government plans to finance 10 percent of its 1997 general budget with the sale of stock in Guatel and other state-owned companies which will be going public.
